1. Description

This pairing examines two aspects of sea level:

  • Global mean sea level change, averaged over the world’s oceans. Global mean or “absolute” sea level represents the height of the ocean surface relative to the center of the Earth.
  • Relative sea level change at specific locations along U.S. coasts. Relative sea level change incorporates changes in the height of the ocean surface as well as vertical land motion (e.g., subsidence, tectonic uplift). Relative sea level is also influenced by the gravitational pull of ice sheets (as they melt, sea level can drop near the ice sheet as its gravitational pull decreases, whereas sea level far from the melting ice sheet will rise faster), changes in currents (the speed of the Atlantic Gulf Stream pulls water away from the coast, so if it slows, sea levels along the coast will rise faster), and other complex interactions. Relative sea level is the sea level change that people and infrastructure along the coast will actually experience.

This feature builds upon EPA’s Sea Level indicator and includes the following components:

  • Historical observations that include a global tide gauge-based reconstruction starting in 1880, local tide gauge data starting in 1960, and satellite measurements of global mean sea level starting in 1993.
  • Projections from 2005 to 2150 for two sea level rise scenarios.
